svg.title: A vPC pair drawn with is peer link, its independent keepalive path and an orphan port, beside the three failures and what each one does
svg.desc: Two switches joined by a peer link, with a keepalive path running through a separate management network above them. A downstream switch dual-homed to both, forming a port channel, and a second downstream switch single-homed to one member, forming an orphan port. A table beside it gives three failures: peer link down suspends the secondary member's vPC ports while keepalive still works, keepalive down changes nothing because the peer link carries the traffic, and both down produces a split brain where both members act active. A note stresses that suspension is protection, not failure, and that the peer link and keepalive must not share a physical path.
svg.text: Two switches that behave as one, and the three ways that behaviour can break
Every feature that removes a blocked port adds a link whose failure must be reasoned about separately
keepalive (L3 / mgmt)
SW-1
vPC primary
SW-2
vPC secondary
peer-link (carries all cross traffic)
ASW-1
dual homed
vPC port-channel: both links forwarding
ASW-B
single homed
orphan port: survives only while SW-1 lives
A port-channel that spans both members is a vPC. A link that lands on one member
only is an orphan, and it inherits that member's fate.
THREE FAILURES, THREE DIFFERENT ANSWERS
1. Peer-link down, keepalive alive
The secondary suspends its vPC ports, so only one member forwards.
Traffic survives, bandwidth halves, and the design is temporarily unprotected.
This is protection working, not a fault to escalate.
2. Keepalive down, peer-link alive
Nothing changes. The peer link still carries cross traffic and still reports
that the peer is alive, so no suspension is justified.
Silent, harmless, and the reason nobody notices for months.
3. Both down: split brain
Each member concludes the other is dead, both become active, and both
answer for the same addresses. Duplicate IP and MAC, then ARP confusion.
This is the only one that needs an outside opinion: a third detector.
The engineering question is not "does clustering work", it is "how does it find out it is alone": peer link, keepalive, BFD, or an orchestration script.
Peer link and keepalive on the same physical path fail together, and case 2 in this chapter is precisely that: one digger, one afternoon, one split brain.
Draw the two paths on a physical diagram before you draw the logical one. If they cross the same duct, the second path is decoration.
Inventory the orphans before every change: a single-homed switch whose uplink sits on the member you are about to reboot goes down quietly,
and the change ticket said "no impact". That is not a networking failure; it is an inventory failure.
